brief: 6 books that quietly changed how I run a company. Why each one mattered.

slots.headline: Six Books That Quietly Changed How I Run a Company

slots.title: Output Over Activity
slots.body: Grove taught me to judge managerial work by output, not hours spent. I stopped counting busywork and started tracking team outcomes. Meetings shrank; decisions accelerated. It remains the clearest framework for operational leverage.

slots.title: Time Is Scarcest
slots.body: Drucker forced me to audit where my hours actually go. I began blocking deep-work windows and delegating everything else. The result was fewer decisions made by fatigue and more made by design.

slots.title: See The System
slots.body: Meadows showed me that every policy creates feedback loops I cannot ignore. I stopped blaming individuals for structural failures. Now I map incentives before I announce new rules, which prevents half the resistance I used to fight.

slots.title: Push Authority Down
slots.body: Marquet proved that intent-based leadership outperforms top-down control. I stopped giving orders and started asking my team to brief me on their decisions. Ownership soared; bottlenecks vanished because clarity replaced permission.

slots.title: Choose Great Over Big
slots.body: Burlingham introduced me to companies that prioritized excellence over endless scale. I redefined our north star around craftsmanship and customer depth. Growth still happens, but only after culture and quality are already locked in.

slots.title: Grow People First
slots.body: Kegan and Lahey convinced me that a company is only as strong as its weakest growth habit. I began building feedback rituals that expose blind spots instead of hiding them. Developing people is developing the business.
